desc:
Mirror a binary tree: swap the left and right child of every node, so that the whole tree is reflected left to right. Return the mirrored tree.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed (or returned) as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree below: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

The result must use the same encoding. For tree = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9] the answer is [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]. For tree = [1, 2, -1, 3] (a chain going down to the left) the answer is [1, -1, 2, -1, 3] (a chain going down to the right).
constraints: Every tree array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Look at what mirroring does to one single node, and then think about what it does to the subtrees below it.
Mirroring a tree means: swap the two children, then mirror the left subtree and mirror the right subtree.
Do it with recursion or an explicit stack/queue that visits every node once. Remember to write the answer back in level-order with -1 for gaps and without trailing -1s.
editorial: The mirror image of a tree is built from the mirror images of its subtrees: the new left child is the mirror of the old right subtree and the new right child is the mirror of the old left subtree. So a single pass that swaps the two children of every node does the whole job, in any visiting order (preorder, postorder or level by level).

With the array encoding the work is mostly bookkeeping. Read the tree into per-node child links, exchange the two link arrays, and write the tree back in level order, dropping the trailing -1 entries. Each node is touched a constant number of times, so the time is linear.
